title: CellScope
summary: A cellphone microscope, from the optical system to the reconstructed image.
role: Founder and optical systems engineer • Computational imaging and optomechanical design
intro: I started CellScope after working with microscopes in my high school biology lab that were outdated and expensive. I wanted to make useful microscopy accessible with equipment people already had. A cellphone was a practical starting point because it provided a camera, display and computing platform in one device.

The phone camera could not provide the imaging performance on its own. I combined it with compact optics and Fourier ptychography, which reconstructs a higher-resolution image from measurements taken under different illumination angles. I implemented the reconstruction in Python, linking the physical acquisition process to the image the user ultimately sees.

sections.title: Requirements and design decisions
paragraphs: Cost was one requirement, but it had to be considered alongside resolution, field of view and acquisition time. A small high-resolution image would limit how much of a specimen someone could inspect. A long acquisition would make the instrument less useful for changing samples. The design needed to balance those requirements across the optics, illumination and reconstruction.

I used angular illumination to collect different spatial-frequency information from the sample. The reconstruction depends on those measurements agreeing with the optical model, so illumination geometry, focus and consistency across the sequence matter. Computation extends what the captured data can reveal; it does not remove the need for a stable, well-characterized instrument.

In the later mechanical design, the phone and optics remain stationary while the lightweight sample stage moves for focus. That reduces the mass the focus mechanism has to control. I also included X–Y positioning and a stage that extends beyond the housing for slide loading. The tradeoff is that the moving stage must provide access while returning to a usable imaging position within the short working distance.

These decisions build on each other. Choosing a phone made the system accessible, but introduced optical limitations. Reconstruction addressed part of that limitation, which made acquisition consistency and mechanical stability more important. I had to design the instrument as a connected system.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: The prototype reported in my 2024 ISEF abstract achieved **2.2 µm resolution across a 2.01 mm² field of view**, with **0.6 seconds of dataset acquisition**, at a cost below C$200. That timing describes collecting the images used for reconstruction. It is not the full processing time.

The project took me to ISEF 2024 and led to a publication on cellphone-based Fourier ptychography through IEEE. Those results describe the research prototype. The later mechanical design is a separate iteration focused on how someone loads, positions and focuses a sample.

title: WaferWatch
summary: Follow the fabrication process. Trace a result back through the steps that produced it.
role: Concept, product design and full implementation • Fabrication workflow software
intro: I conceived and built WaferWatch because I wanted an accessible, transparent way to understand the entire fabrication pipeline. When a problem appears in a wafer or die, the result alone does not explain where the mistake happened. I wanted researchers to be able to follow the chain of work, inspect the relevant steps and investigate where an error may have entered the process.

I owned the project from the idea through the interface, application logic and implementation. WaferWatch brings process plans, wafer and die movement, checkpoints, parameters, inspections and scheduling into a shared application built with Next.js, TypeScript, Supabase and PostgreSQL.

sections.title: Making the process understandable
paragraphs: The interface needed to work at two levels. Researchers need an overview of the full process, but they also need to inspect what happened to one particular wafer or die. I organized the application around a process view connected to individual histories, so the overview and the underlying evidence remain part of the same workflow.

The most important data-model decision was to keep the intended process separate from its actual execution. A published plan describes what should happen. An operation run records a particular instance of that work. If a step is repeated, or work splits into separate paths, it receives a distinct linked identity instead of overwriting the previous visit.

That costs more schema and transition logic than storing a single current status. It also preserves the information needed to compare conditions before and after a problem. A correction should make the record more accurate without making the original event disappear, so checkpoint history is append-only and corrections supersede earlier evidence.

sections.title: Keeping the record consistent
paragraphs: I kept movement eligibility on the server. A connection drawn in the interface describes the process, but it is not enough to authorize a change. Server actions, project permissions, revision checks and idempotency protections keep duplicate or out-of-order requests from silently changing the history.

The process view, planning views and wafer status use shared projections of the same underlying work. Realtime updates carry ordered changes, with a new snapshot when a client has missed part of the retained history. This makes collaboration a data-consistency problem as well as an interface problem.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: The result is an implemented application for following fabrication work and inspecting the evidence around individual steps. I also built verification mechanisms for lifecycle transitions, checkpoints, permissions, collaboration and data migrations. The system supports investigating where an error occurred; identifying the actual cause still depends on the measurements and process evidence. Its core contribution is making that history accessible without losing the details needed to investigate it.

title: FRIDAY
summary: Scan a room, arrange it with an agent, and keep the design grounded in the space.
role: 3D environment development lead • Room scanning, agent constraints, UI and commerce integration
intro: FRIDAY began at HackMIT as a way to design a room with an AI agent in a shared 3D environment. I led development of the environment and worked on adapting the visual-odometry and reconstruction system for room scanning. I wanted people to use their own spaces, making the experience accessible beyond rooms we had prepared ourselves.

I also helped constrain the agent system and its domain-specific language, worked on the website UI, and contributed to the Visa Intelligent Commerce integration and transaction pipeline. It was a team effort connecting scanned spaces to products users could inspect and arrange.

sections.title: A room needs more than a convincing image
paragraphs: The environment combines room meshes or Gaussian splats with editable furniture. A reconstruction can look convincing while its scale or boundaries are unsuitable for reliable placement. The application needs dimensions, orientation and support relationships to determine where an item can fit.

Accessible capture creates a tradeoff with calibration. Phone video is easy to obtain, but the result still needs usable spatial information. The phone-video reconstruction path remains experimental, with manual integration. The active editor uses PlayCanvas to render rooms and manipulate furniture.

sections.title: Constraining the agent
paragraphs: The agent needed to operate within both product constraints and spatial constraints. A request can include a budget, material, dimensions or relationships between items. I helped define those requirements so they could be represented explicitly instead of existing only in a prompt.

Natural-language search is compiled into a validated constraint language for deterministic filtering. Scene changes are staged and checked against geometry and revision state before being committed. The agent can inspect the scene and request screenshots tied to a particular revision, which helps keep its reasoning connected to the room the user is actually editing.

sections.title: Connecting a design to products
paragraphs: My commerce work addressed how companies or communities could expose their products as 3D models in the same environment. Product identity has to remain consistent from the model and catalogue listing through the selected design and cart. The checkout path uses an immutable snapshot, explicit approval and MFA before Visa sandbox submission.

The implementation includes catalogue discovery, editable arrangements and a transaction path ending at a sandbox receipt. Together, these support the goal of evaluating a design in someone’s own space and understanding the products being selected.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: Our team finished **Top 12 overall and third in the OpenAI 5th Teammate Challenge at HackMIT 2026**. FRIDAY brought together an interactive room editor, bounded agent tools and a product workflow that users could compare and revise.

title: HALO
summary: Connecting wearable data and local inference on a real phone.
role: Wearable integration, edge inference and clinical-record connection • Android prototype
intro: My work on HALO connected wearable data, on-device inference and hospital information. The goal was to give an assistant useful health context on a phone, where someone could see their data and ask questions without treating every reading as an isolated number.

I worked on the integration between the data and model paths. The Android application uses Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, local storage, Health Connect and an ExecuTorch/Qualcomm QNN model path. I integrated and debugged the application on a Samsung S25 Ultra.

sections.title: Combining records with different meanings
paragraphs: A wearable reading and a clinical record are not interchangeable. They may describe different time periods, have different units or arrive at different rates. The system needs to distinguish a recent measurement from a historical observation, and missing data from a normal result.

The wearable path includes Health Connect permissions and record queries. For clinical information, the FHIR connection reads Patient, Observation and Condition resources. The prototype’s FHIR configuration targets a demo server, so this work demonstrates the integration path rather than a deployed connection to a hospital’s live records.

That separation matters to the interface as well. An answer should remain connected to the data available for that person and time period. Combining sources is only useful when the application retains enough context to explain what it is using.

sections.title: Working within the phone
paragraphs: On-device inference introduced a different set of constraints from calling a hosted model. Prompt size, generated output and concurrent requests all affect memory use and responsiveness. The local service bounds the prompt and response, serializes generation with a mutex and loads the model through ExecuTorch/QNN.

I also had to account for incomplete context and failures. The service includes cleanup and fallback paths for missing data, invalid output and inference errors. A fallback is a different outcome from a model-generated answer, and the application needs to preserve that distinction.

Local generation does not mean the whole application is offline. Imported clinical records and external tool requests have their own boundaries. I treat the location of inference, data retrieval and tool execution as separate parts of the architecture.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: HALO became an Android prototype bringing wearable and clinical-data paths into a shared application with a local inference implementation. My work included real-device integration and debugging across the model, data and UI paths. The prototype establishes those engineering connections, with clinical-record access configured against a demo server.

title: Lithium niobate photonics
summary: Waveguide-bend design tied to a fabrication platform and a fair simulation comparison.
role: Undergraduate photonics research • Waveguide geometry and simulation workflow
intro: In my photonics work at McMaster, I’ve worked on lithium niobate waveguide design using Ansys Lumerical and LumOpt. The bend study connects optical simulation to a specific fabrication platform. The geometry needs to represent the material stack and etch profile that the device could actually have.

The active configuration uses X-cut lithium niobate at a wavelength of 1550 nm, with a 600 nm film, a 300 nm etch and an 800 nm waveguide top width. The model includes 70-degree sidewalls and a 4.7 µm buried-oxide layer. Those dimensions constrain the design rather than serving as details added after optimization.

sections.title: Representing the fabricated cross section
paragraphs: An etched ridge has a trapezoidal cross section, so the top and bottom widths are different. I used the etch depth and sidewall angle to define that shape consistently. Modeling an ideal rectangular core would change the confinement and could make an optimization result less representative of the intended device.

Lithium niobate is also anisotropic. The crystal orientation and propagation direction affect the material response seen by a mode. The simulation therefore needs a consistent relationship between the index tensor, geometry and mode convention. A bend changes the propagation direction, which makes those conventions especially important.

sections.title: Balancing design freedom and simulation cost
paragraphs: The implemented optimization path uses three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulation with LumOpt. It can evaluate the full geometry, but that comes with substantial computational cost. The project also defines a proposed faster stage using mode solving and eigenmode expansion; that remains separate from the active FDTD path.

A more compact or more complicated bend is only useful if it improves the relevant optical result under a fair comparison. Ports, modes, normalization, mesh treatment and boundaries need to remain consistent between the baseline and candidate. The 20 nm design-mesh setting is an input to that comparison, not evidence that it has converged.

sections.title: Result and current stage
paragraphs: The work has produced a fabrication-aware model and an implemented workflow for exploring waveguide-bend designs. It also connects to fabrication-support documents and layout work. At this stage, the optical results are simulation results, and a measured device result would require fabrication and optical characterization.

The main engineering outcome is a design process tied to a defined platform. It makes the assumptions explicit enough that a candidate geometry can be evaluated against the same physical and numerical conditions as its reference.

title: HackerFab stepper
summary: Working through the illumination, focus and motion requirements of maskless lithography.
role: Stepper design and refactoring • Optical design study
intro: My HackerFab work covers lithography stepper design and refactoring. The stepper study explores maskless pattern transfer using a digital micromirror device and reduction optics. I’m working through how the illumination, projected pattern and positioning system fit together, with the optical requirements informing the mechanical ones.

The studied configuration uses 410 nm illumination, a DLP471TP and a 10× objective with numerical aperture 0.25. It gives a calculated projected field of approximately 1.04 × 0.58 mm and a projected pixel pitch of about 0.54 µm.

sections.title: Sampling and resolution
paragraphs: One important distinction is that projected pixel size is not the same as printable feature size. The optical study estimates an Airy diameter of roughly 2 µm. Smaller projected pixels can sample that response, but they do not remove diffraction, aberration or the effect of the resist process.

I therefore treat the projected grid, optical response and resulting resist pattern as separate parts of the design. A useful exposure system needs all three to agree, and the final feature size has to be established with a process test.

sections.title: Throughput and focus tolerance
paragraphs: Reduction also affects how much light reaches the sample. With the assumed illumination cone and numerical aperture, the study estimates that only about 0.8–1.1% of that cone is accepted. This ties the optical layout to dose and exposure time. A choice that gives a smaller projected field can make the illumination problem harder.

The estimated depth of focus is approximately ±3.3 µm. That is a mechanical requirement as well as an optical quantity: substrate tilt, stage flatness and Z motion all use part of the available focus tolerance. Positioning between exposures adds another constraint, because nominal motor resolution does not establish repeatability or account for backlash.
The tradeoff is between field size, optical detail, available dose and positioning difficulty. Optimizing one number in isolation would hide the requirements placed on the rest of the system.

sections.title: Result and current stage
paragraphs: My contribution includes the stepper design work and refactoring. The optical study makes the design assumptions and calculated limits explicit, giving the build a basis for discussing illumination, focus and motion requirements.

The values above are calculated design quantities. They are not measured resist resolution or demonstrated positioning accuracy. The next experimental stage is to connect the optical model to field-uniformity measurements, focus sweeps, printed patterns and repeated stage motion.

title: Laser diode current driver
summary: Choosing a first-board architecture around current quality, heat and independent protection.
role: Architecture design study • Current control, protection and thermal design
intro: I developed an architecture study for an adjustable laser-diode current source powered from an existing 12 V supply. The documented operating range is 0–3.5 A, with independent protection below the diode’s 4 A absolute limit. The problem was to choose a practical first-board architecture while balancing current quality, heat, cost and control complexity.

I compared a direct synchronous buck driver with a switching preregulator followed by a precision linear stage. The hybrid architecture offered a route to quieter current, but added dissipation and another control loop. The comparison recommended a TPS92640 direct-buck design for the first board, with a bypassable linear post-stage available for comparison.

sections.title: Current quality and thermal design
paragraphs: I considered ripple and drift separately. Switching behavior and layout affect short-timescale variation. Reference stability, shunt temperature and thermal coupling affect slower changes. Improving one does not necessarily improve the other, so the architecture needs a clear measurement path as well as a current command.

The proposed control path uses a 16-bit DAC, a precision reference, a low-temperature-coefficient Kelvin shunt and independent current measurement. The architecture calls for a power stage rated for at least 5 A, while the normal command remains limited to 3.5 A. The additional component rating provides margin; it does not raise the allowed laser current.

Driver heat also interacts with the temperature-control system. In the architecture, I separated the filtered laser and thermoelectric-cooler supply branches and directed driver dissipation toward the chassis rather than the TEC cold side. A linear stage can improve current quality while making that thermal burden worse.

sections.title: Protection and architecture selection
paragraphs: The design calls for an independent hardware shutdown or overcurrent latch, with a proposed trip range of 3.65–3.75 A. Protection should not depend entirely on the software setting the current correctly.

The hybrid option scored highest in the weighted comparison, but the direct buck was the recommended first build. That choice reduces initial complexity while preserving a way to test whether the added linear stage is necessary. The decision depends on measured behavior at the actual load, rather than assuming the more elaborate architecture is automatically the better system.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: The outcome is a documented set of requirements, an architecture comparison and a first-board recommendation. This remains a pre-prototype design study. Current accuracy, ripple, thermal drift and fault behavior still require characterization, beginning with a dummy load before connecting the laser.

title: FSD / camera perception
summary: Turning camera observations into a spatial scene, with controlled experiments behind the picture.
role: Perception research and experimental evaluation • Six-camera nuScenes pipeline
intro: I’ve been developing a camera-based perception pipeline and testing how changes to its architecture and training affect the result. The six-camera nuScenes implementation predicts car and pedestrian boxes together with road and sidewalk outputs. I’m interested in improving the system while retaining enough experimental control to understand why a change helped or failed.

The work includes proposal selection, quality scoring, yaw supervision, feature injection and training-recipe experiments. A central requirement is that a candidate has to improve against a matched control, rather than only producing a promising screenshot or a better result on a small screening set.

sections.title: Keeping comparisons meaningful
paragraphs: Branches start from the same checkpoint, with checks on retained tensors, optimizer state and resumability. I keep the original task scope in the comparison: both object classes and the road and sidewalk outputs. Removing a difficult class or reducing the perception range would change the problem being evaluated.

I also separate ranking changes from geometric changes. For example, a quality-scoring comparison should use identical boxes when testing whether a score improves precision at matched recall. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to tell whether the improvement came from the ranking or the underlying predictions.
Latency and memory have to be measured under the same six-camera configuration. A timing result for one module does not establish the frame rate of the complete pipeline.

sections.title: A result that did not justify adoption
paragraphs: In the recorded September 13 campaign, lowering the restart learning rate avoided the larger regression caused by the higher rate. On full validation, car BEV AP50 changed from 37.46% for the retained epoch-18 model to 37.50% for the selected lower-rate continuation. Pedestrian BEV AP50 changed from 2.02% to 1.92%.

That did not satisfy the declared mean object-AP improvement rule, so I retained epoch 18. The small car improvement was not enough to justify replacing the model. These were custom research metrics, and I do not present them as official nuScenes NDS or a sealed-test result.

sections.title: Current research scope
paragraphs: The later campaign03 plan sets out full-epoch comparisons for additional hypotheses, including corner supervision, higher-resolution lifting and audited object-surface depth targets. Those hypotheses remain distinct from the dated results above.
This project focuses on perception. The work has produced an implemented pipeline, controlled experiment branches and a record of decisions about which changes were supported by the evidence.

title: Astronomy in the cold
summary: Understanding the gap between cold hands and the fine adjustments a telescope requires.
role: Praxis II team project • Stakeholder research, problem framing and requirements
intro: In Praxis II, our team worked with the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada on the difficulty of operating telescopes in cold weather. We investigated a mismatch between the dexterity observers could maintain in the cold and the fine control their equipment required. Gloves could preserve warmth while making small adjustments harder, but removing them exposed the fingers needed for those adjustments.

Our research included conversations with RASC members, contact with our primary stakeholder and observation of the tasks involved in telescope use. We also looked at how people in other settings handled the same conflict between warmth and manual control.

sections.title: Framing the problem before choosing a device
paragraphs: We kept two approaches open: preserve hand function in the cold, or reduce the dexterity the telescope requires. That gave us room to consider heating, hand protection, control adaptations and changes to the interaction, instead of committing immediately to a heated glove.

The requirements focused on observing tasks. We defined a micro-task protocol and set a target for task time no greater than 1.5 times the control condition. The design also had to work in low light without requiring bright or white-light activation, and avoid requiring bare-skin contact with cold metal.

We considered the telescope as part of the thermal system. Heat near the optical path can disturb observing quality, so the report included a target of no more than a 10% increase in stellar-image width relative to a comparable baseline. Proposed cold conditioning at −15 °C, a 2 kg added-mass limit and an 8 L packed-volume limit connected the concept to winter use and transport.

sections.title: What changed the design space
paragraphs: Protective handlebar muffs used by delivery riders helped us think about alternating between warmth and dexterity. A person does not necessarily need the same hand configuration throughout the entire activity. That informed our exploration of a concept that provides warmth when needed and allows less obstructed movement for precise tasks.

The tradeoff was therefore broader than insulation thickness. We had to consider how often an observer transitions between modes, how difficult that transition is with cold hands, and whether it introduces another interruption to observing.

sections.title: Outcome
paragraphs: We developed a requirements report grounded in the community’s workflow and used it to broaden and evaluate the concept space. The targets define success for subsequent prototype validation. The completed work described here is our problem framing, stakeholder research and concept development.

title: The Bifröst
summary: A matboard bridge shaped by moving loads, buckling and a fixed material budget.
role: CIV102 team project • Structural analysis and matboard bridge construction
intro: I worked with Michael Mao Li, Beckett Deschamps and Jeffrey Hu to design and construct The Bifröst, a matboard bridge for CIV102. We had a 1200 mm span, a limited sheet of 1.27 mm matboard and prescribed moving train loads. Our goal was to predict the governing failure mode and improve load capacity while keeping the bridge practical to fabricate.

We began by analyzing the reference cross section, then revised the geometry, flange reinforcement and diaphragm layout. Hand calculations and MATLAB and Python analysis let us compare bending, shear and buckling under the moving load envelope.

sections.title: Working within the material budget
paragraphs: A deeper section increases the second moment of area, but it also changes web stability. More material in the compression flange can help that failure mode while leaving less material for other reinforcement. We treated those changes as a coupled design problem instead of optimizing each dimension separately.

Fabrication constrained the analysis. A design had to fit on the available matboard and leave workable connections and glue tabs. Geometric efficiency was only useful if we could cut and assemble it accurately enough to realize the assumed section.

sections.title: Placing reinforcement where it mattered
paragraphs: We investigated unequal diaphragm spacing using the shear envelope and thin-plate buckling relationships. The layout preserved required support and center constraints while placing reinforcement according to the demand along the span. That provided a way to use the available material more deliberately than applying one spacing everywhere.
The final report describes a 160 mm tall pi-beam with a 100 mm double-layer top flange, two webs spaced 60 mm apart and an unequal diaphragm layout.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: We constructed the bridge and predicted compression failure at **1.367 kN**. That value is an analytical prediction, not a measured failure load. Our model did not fully capture glue variability or cutting and assembly errors, which matter when transferring the calculated geometry into a physical structure.
The project connected structural analysis to a fabrication constraint I could see directly: every reinforcement choice had to fit into the same sheet and survive the way we assembled it.

title: A quieter can opening
summary: Comparing ways to release pressure while preserving portability, cleanliness and the drink.
role: Praxis I team project • Mechanism design and prototype comparison
intro: Our Praxis I team investigated how to make a beverage can easier and quieter to open while retaining portability, cleanliness and the drink itself. We compared several approaches, including a needle-and-straw concept, opening under water, a rubber tab and a slider-based opening.

The requirements extended beyond sound. A concept also had to consider opening effort, sharp edges, contamination, cleaning and liquid loss. A quieter opening would not be useful if the mechanism made the can difficult to carry or introduced a new handling problem.

sections.title: Using uncertainty to guide testing
paragraphs: We used pairwise comparisons and Pugh charts to narrow the concepts, then moved the uncertain comparisons into prototype testing. A question mark in the chart identified something we needed evidence for, such as whether a rubber sleeve would meaningfully change the acoustic response or whether a new opening would lose more liquid.

Shupeng Liu led the Pugh charts and convergence analysis. Our team’s subsequent comparisons examined sound, opening force and pressure, liquid retention, portability and cleaning. That allowed the final selection to draw on measured prototype behavior as well as the initial qualitative assessment.

sections.title: Changing the opening mechanism
paragraphs: The slider concept changed how the can opened by removing the scored-ligament fracture mechanism and controlling the vent area. That addressed the opening event directly, instead of depending only on damping around the existing tab.

The change also affected sealing, exposed area and the force needed to operate the opening. Those interactions mattered because controlling pressure release could influence sound and beverage loss at the same time. The tradeoff was a more substantial change to the can architecture, with manufacturing and sealing questions that a simple accessory would avoid.

sections.title: Result
paragraphs: Our prototype comparison favored the slider across the project’s main criteria and supported selecting it as the final concept. The outcome was a coursework prototype; manufacturing, long-term sealing and food-contact suitability remain questions for further development.
The useful result was a traceable design decision: we moved from several plausible mechanisms to a selected concept by testing the uncertainties that mattered to the requirements.

title: Jungle
summary: Browser-testing agents with inspectable history, approval gates and replay.
role: GenAI Genesis 2026 • Two-person team • Agent runtime and test workflows
intro: I co-developed Jungle as a desktop runtime for agents that generate, execute, critique and replay browser tests. I worked on approval gates, persistent run histories and artifacts, branching and replay, and a portable agentic CLI. The system uses Electron, Playwright, Python, Langflow and MySQL.

sections.title: Design decisions and outcome
paragraphs: A generated test needs more than a final pass or fail message. Someone has to be able to inspect what was attempted, what happened in the browser and how the run reached that state. I built around persistent execution history so a failed attempt could remain available for comparison instead of being replaced by the next run.

Branching and replay support iteration from that record. Approval gates provide a point of control before an agent proceeds through a guarded action. These features add state-management complexity, but make the runtime easier to inspect when an agent behaves unexpectedly.

The result was a sandboxed test runtime with inspectable histories and recovery-oriented workflows. It does not establish that a model-generated test is correct simply because it executes. Generation, execution and critique remain separate parts of the process.

title: Wicker
summary: A voice-to-3D pipeline for pose references that can be manipulated with hand tracking.
role: Hack the North 2025 • Team AR project • Generation and integration pipeline
intro: Hack the North was my first hackathon. I arrived without a team and met teammates on the bus from Toronto to Waterloo. We shared an interest in augmented reality, which became Wicker: an AR pose-reference system for artists that generates 3D models from voice prompts and lets the user manipulate their pose through hand tracking.

sections.title: Design decisions and outcome
paragraphs: I worked on the pipeline connecting generation, rigging, storage and the AR interaction. The project integrated Snap3D, Meshy AI and AWS using Node.js, Python and TypeScript. A generated mesh had to become an asset the application could load and manipulate, so the boundaries between services mattered as much as any individual API.

The design separates slower asset preparation from interactive posing. Once a model is available, manipulating it needs a responsive interaction loop rather than another generation request. The result was a prototype connecting a spoken idea to an editable AR reference, with the integration between stages forming much of the engineering work.

title: Looky
summary: Extending QuickLookStep with geometry selection, measurement and repeatable diagnostics.
role: QuickLookStep fork • Geometry interaction and diagnostics
intro: I extended an existing macOS model viewer and Quick Look project with geometry import, selection, measurement and diagnostics. My work used SwiftUI, SceneKit and Metal, including CPU bounding-volume-hierarchy logic for picking edges and surfaces.

sections.title: Design decisions and outcome
paragraphs: Selection has to remain consistent across the imported geometry, scene coordinates and the point the user indicates on screen. A model that renders correctly can still produce the wrong selection or measurement if those representations disagree. I added diagnostic workflows and replayable tests around selection accuracy and coordinate mapping so those errors could be examined repeatedly.

The result is my extended Looky fork of QuickLookStep. My contributions build on the original viewer, adding more detailed geometry interaction and repeatable ways to investigate selection and measurement behavior.

title: Newmux
summary: Recoverable terminal state, soft deletion and restoration around Ghostty and tmux.
role: Terminal workflow development • Recoverable state and regression testing
intro: I built Newmux around Ghostty and tmux workflows, focusing on recoverable terminal state. The implementation supports soft deletion, restoration and history, with build and regression scripts covering terminal, tab, session, keyboard and restore behavior.

sections.title: Design decisions and outcome
paragraphs: Recovery changes what a close or delete action means. The system needs to retain enough state to restore the intended context while keeping the visible session understandable. That creates a tradeoff between simple immediate deletion and a more explicit lifecycle for recoverable objects.

My work centered on those state transitions and their regression behavior. The result is a workflow distribution with explicit history and restoration features around the terminal session, backed by checks for the transitions most likely to break recovery.

title: FrameGen
summary: An early implementation for experimenting with frame interpolation and evaluation.
role: Early frame-interpolation project • Model and processing scaffolding
intro: I created scaffolding for a frame-interpolation project, covering model configuration, training and frame processing. The aim is to estimate intermediate frames from an input sequence, which creates a tradeoff between visual quality and the cost of inference.

sections.title: Design decisions and outcome
paragraphs: The outcome of this stage is the implementation scaffolding for experimenting with that pipeline. Model configuration, training and frame processing are represented in the project, while a reproducible comparison of image quality and inference performance remains a separate evaluation task.
